subproblem.title: Countable uniformly dense family of test functions supported in a compact set
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type u) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [SecondCountableTopology X] (K : Set X), IsCompact K → ∃ D : Set C_c(X, ℝ), D.Countable ∧ (∀ g ∈ D, tsupport g ⊆ K) ∧ ∀ f : C_c(X, ℝ), tsupport f ⊆ K → ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ g ∈ D, ∀ x, |f x - g x| ≤ ε
subproblem.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `rc_cc_countable_dense`.
Source: the parent proof of Simon Thm 4.16 (corrected), Step 1: “Each K_j is a compact metrizable space (X is metrizable), so C(K_j) is separable; choose a countable dense set 𝒟_j ⊆ C(K_j)”. Here it is specialized to the restrictions of test functions supported in K, which is all that Steps 4–5 use.

Notation.
- C(K) is the set of continuous u : K → ℝ (K with the subspace topology), with the sup distance d(u, v) := sup_{y∈K} |u(y) − v(y)|. This is finite because K is compact; if K = ∅, C(K) has one element.
- S := {f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) : tsupport f ⊆ K}, and r : S → C(K) is the restriction r(f) := f|_K.

1. K is compact metrizable. With the subspace topology K is compact and Hausdorff, and it is second countable (a countable base of X restricts to a countable base of K). A compact Hausdorff space is normal, hence regular, and a regular second countable space is metrizable (Urysohn metrization). So K is compact metrizable; fix a compatible metric ρ on K.
2. C(K) is separable. This is trivial if K = ∅; otherwise:
   - K, being compact metric, is separable: for each m ≥ 1, finitely many ρ-balls of radius 1/m cover K, and the collection of all their centres is countable and dense. Let {y_n : n ∈ ℕ} be dense in K and h_n(y) := ρ(y, y_n), so h_n ∈ C(K).
   - The family (h_n) separates points. If y ≠ y′, put δ := ρ(y, y′) > 0 and choose n with ρ(y, y_n) < δ/2. Then h_n(y) < δ/2 < δ − ρ(y, y_n) ≤ ρ(y′, y_n) = h_n(y′).
   - The real subalgebra of C(K) generated by the constant 1 and the h_n contains the constants and separates points, so it is dense in C(K) by the Stone–Weierstrass theorem.
   - The countable set Q of polynomials with rational coefficients in finitely many of the h_n is dense in that subalgebra. Each h_n is bounded, so in the sup distance a polynomial expression in h_1, …, h_N depends continuously on its finitely many coefficients.
   - Hence Q is dense in C(K), and C(K) is separable. This is the standard fact quoted in the parent proof: C(K) is separable for compact metrizable K.
3. The subset r(S) is separable. Let Q be countable and dense in the metric space C(K), and Y := r(S).
   - For every pair (q, s) ∈ Q × ℚ_{>0} for which the open ball B(q, s) meets Y, choose y_{q,s} ∈ B(q, s) ∩ Y. Let T be the countable set of these points, so T ⊆ Y.
   - T is dense in Y. Given y ∈ Y and ε > 0, choose a rational s ∈ (0, ε/2) and q ∈ Q with d(q, y) < s. Then B(q, s) meets Y (it contains y), and d(y, y_{q,s}) ≤ d(y, q) + d(q, y_{q,s}) < 2s < ε.
   - Thus T ⊆ r(S) is countable and r(S) ⊆ closure(T).
4. The family D. For every t ∈ T choose g_t ∈ S with r(g_t) = t, and let D := {g_t : t ∈ T}. D is countable (an image of the countable set T), and every g ∈ D lies in S, i.e. tsupport g ⊆ K.
5. Uniform approximation. Let f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) with tsupport f ⊆ K, and let ε > 0. Then f ∈ S and r(f) ∈ r(S) ⊆ closure(T), so there is t ∈ T with d(r(f), t) < ε. Put g := g_t ∈ D, so r(g) = t.
   - For x ∈ K: |f(x) − g(x)| = |r(f)(x) − r(g)(x)| ≤ d(r(f), r(g)) = d(r(f), t) < ε.
   - For x ∉ K: x ∉ tsupport f and x ∉ tsupport g (both are contained in K), so f(x) = 0 = g(x) and |f(x) − g(x)| = 0 < ε.
   Hence |f(x) − g(x)| ≤ ε for every x ∈ X. ∎

subproblem.title: Test functions are integrable against a Radon outer measure
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type u) [TopologicalSpace X] (μ : OuterMeasure X), IsRadonOuterMeasure μ → ∀ f : C_c(X, ℝ), Integrable (fun x => f x) (caratheodoryMeasure μ)
subproblem.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `rc_cc_integrable`.
Source: the parent proof of Simon Thm 4.16 (corrected), Step 3: “Each f ∈ C_c(X) is μ_k-integrable (bounded, continuous, support compact of finite measure)”. Here it is stated for a single Radon outer measure μ on an arbitrary topological space.

Notation (Lemma 1.6/Remark 1.7).
- 𝓜_μ is the σ-algebra of μ-measurable sets (Carathéodory: A ∈ 𝓜_μ iff μ(E) = μ(E ∩ A) + μ(E ∖ A) for every E ⊆ X).
- μ̄ = caratheodoryMeasure μ is the measure on (X, 𝓜_μ) with μ̄(A) = μ(A) for A ∈ 𝓜_μ.
- Fix f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) and put S := tsupport f, the closure of {x : f(x) ≠ 0}.

1. Borel sets are μ-measurable. By (R1), μ is Borel regular. The first half of Borel regularity says that every Borel subset of X lies in 𝓜_μ; in particular every open set and every closed set lies in 𝓜_μ.
2. f is 𝓜_μ-measurable. For each open V ⊆ ℝ the set f⁻¹(V) is open (f is continuous), hence in 𝓜_μ by Step 1. The open sets generate the Borel σ-algebra of ℝ, so f is 𝓜_μ-measurable. As ℝ is second countable, f is therefore strongly measurable for μ̄.
3. The support has finite measure. S is closed (it is a closure) and compact (f has compact support). By Step 1, S ∈ 𝓜_μ, so μ̄(S) = μ(S). By the finiteness clause of (R1), μ(S) < ∞.
4. f is dominated by a multiple of 1_S. If S = ∅, put C := 0. Otherwise f is continuous on the nonempty compact set S, so |f| attains a maximum C ≥ 0 on S. For x ∉ S we have f(x) = 0, because x is not in the set {f ≠ 0} whose closure is S. Hence |f(x)| ≤ C·1_S(x) for every x ∈ X.
5. Conclusion. By Steps 3–4, ∫_X |f| dμ̄ ≤ C·μ̄(S) = C·μ(S) < ∞. Together with Step 2, f is μ̄-integrable. ∎

- Set `letI : MeasurableSpace X := μ.caratheodory`.
- Get `OpensMeasurableSpace X` from `hμ.borel_regular.borel_le_caratheodory`.
- Get `IsFiniteMeasureOnCompacts (caratheodoryMeasure μ)` from SimonGMT `hμ.toCaratheodoryMeasure_apply_all K` (RadonOuterMeasure.lean) together with `hμ.finite_compacts`. `hμ.toCaratheodoryMeasure` and `caratheodoryMeasure μ` are the same abbreviation, so the rewrite works via `show … from …`.
- Conclude with `f.continuous.integrable_of_hasCompactSupport f.hasCompactSupport` (Mathlib MeasureTheory/Function/LocallyIntegrable.lean:622).
proof_key_steps: (R1) Borel regularity puts every Borel set, in particular every open and closed set, in the Carathéodory σ-algebra 𝓜_μ.
f is continuous, hence 𝓜_μ-measurable and strongly measurable for μ̄.
S = tsupport f is closed and compact, so S ∈ 𝓜_μ and μ̄(S) = μ(S) < ∞ by (R1).
|f| ≤ C·1_S with C the maximum of |f| on S (C = 0 if S = ∅).
∫|f| dμ̄ ≤ C·μ(S) < ∞, so f is μ̄-integrable.

subproblem.title: Diagonal subsequence for countably many bounded real sequences
subproblem.statement: Let ι be a countable type (universe u) and let a_k(i) ∈ ℝ (k ∈ ℕ, i ∈ ι). Suppose that for every i ∈ ι the sequence (a_k(i))_{k∈ℕ} is bounded, i.e. there is C_i ∈ ℝ with |a_k(i)| ≤ C_i for all k. Then there is a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ such that for every i ∈ ι the sequence (a_{φ(k)}(i))_{k∈ℕ} converges in ℝ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (ι : Type u) [Countable ι] (a : ℕ → ι → ℝ), (∀ i, ∃ C : ℝ, ∀ k, |a k i| ≤ C) → ∃ φ : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono φ ∧ ∀ i, ∃ l : ℝ, Tendsto (fun k => a (φ k) i) atTop (𝓝 l)
subproblem.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `rc_diagonal_subseq`.
Source: the parent proof of Simon Thm 4.16 (corrected), Step 4: “By Bolzano–Weierstrass choose successively infinite sets ℕ ⊇ N_1 ⊇ N_2 ⊇ ⋯ such that (F_{j_p,k}(g_p))_{k∈N_p} converges, and let φ(k) be the k-th element of N_k … Then φ is strictly increasing … and (φ(k))_{k≥p} is a sequence in N_p”. Here it is written with strictly increasing maps (N_p = ψ_p(ℕ)) for an abstract countable family of bounded sequences.

Standard facts used:
- (a) A strictly increasing σ : ℕ → ℕ satisfies σ(n) ≥ n for every n (induction: σ(0) ≥ 0 and σ(n+1) > σ(n) ≥ n).
- (b) A composition of strictly increasing maps ℕ → ℕ is strictly increasing.
- (c) If x_n → L in ℝ and τ : ℕ → ℕ is strictly increasing, then x_{τ(n)} → L.
- (d) Bolzano–Weierstrass: every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence.

1. Trivial case and enumeration. If ι is empty, φ := id is strictly increasing and the convergence claim is vacuous. Otherwise ι is countable and nonempty, so there is a surjection e : ℕ → ι. For p ∈ ℕ put b_p(k) := a_k(e(p)). By hypothesis |b_p(k)| ≤ C_{e(p)} for all k.
2. Successive subsequences.
   - By (d), choose a strictly increasing σ_0 with (b_0(σ_0(m)))_m convergent, and put ψ_0 := σ_0.
   - Given a strictly increasing ψ_{p−1} (p ≥ 1), the sequence (b_p(ψ_{p−1}(m)))_m is bounded by C_{e(p)}. By (d) there is a strictly increasing σ_p with (b_p(ψ_{p−1}(σ_p(m))))_m convergent. Put ψ_p := ψ_{p−1} ∘ σ_p, which is strictly increasing by (b).
   - By recursion this gives strictly increasing ψ_0, ψ_1, … with ψ_p = ψ_{p−1} ∘ σ_p, and limits L_p := lim_m b_p(ψ_p(m)) for every p. In the parent's notation, N_p := ψ_p(ℕ) is a decreasing sequence of infinite sets along which b_p converges.
3. The diagonal map is strictly increasing. Define φ(m) := ψ_m(m). Then φ(m+1) = ψ_m(σ_{m+1}(m+1)) ≥ ψ_m(m+1) > ψ_m(m) = φ(m). This uses σ_{m+1}(m+1) ≥ m+1 by (a), and that ψ_m is strictly increasing (in particular monotone).
4. Each b_p converges along φ. Fix p.
   - For m ≥ p let ρ_m := σ_{p+1} ∘ ⋯ ∘ σ_m (with ρ_p := id). It is strictly increasing by (b), and ψ_m = ψ_p ∘ ρ_m.
   - Put τ(m) := ρ_m(m) for m ≥ p. Then φ(m) = ψ_p(τ(m)).
   - Since ρ_{m+1} = ρ_m ∘ σ_{m+1}, we get τ(m+1) = ρ_m(σ_{m+1}(m+1)) ≥ ρ_m(m+1) > ρ_m(m) = τ(m), by (a) and strict monotonicity of ρ_m.
   - Hence (b_p(φ(p+n)))_{n∈ℕ} = (b_p(ψ_p(τ(p+n))))_n is a subsequence of the convergent sequence (b_p(ψ_p(n)))_n, so it converges to L_p by (c).
   - Dropping the finitely many terms with index < p does not affect convergence, so b_p(φ(m)) → L_p as m → ∞.
5. Conclusion. Let i ∈ ι and choose p with e(p) = i. Then a_{φ(m)}(i) = b_p(φ(m)) → L_p. So φ is strictly increasing and (a_{φ(k)}(i))_k converges for every i ∈ ι. ∎

Formalization note (non-binding; elaborated in a scratch check, standard axioms only). The same conclusion is the sequential compactness of a countable product of compact intervals.
- With C_i from the hypothesis, every a_k lies in the compact set `Set.pi univ (fun i => Icc (-C i) (C i))` ⊆ ι → ℝ (`isCompact_univ_pi`, `abs_le`).
- ι → ℝ is first countable for countable ι (Topology/Bases.lean:781).
- `IsCompact.tendsto_subseq` (Topology/Sequences.lean:298) then yields φ and b with a ∘ φ → b.
- `((continuous_apply i).tendsto b).comp` gives the coordinatewise limits.
proof_key_steps: Empty ι is trivial; otherwise enumerate ι by a surjection e : ℕ → ι and set b_p(k) = a_k(e(p)).
Recursively choose strictly increasing ψ_p = ψ_{p−1} ∘ σ_p with b_p ∘ ψ_p convergent (Bolzano–Weierstrass).
The diagonal φ(m) = ψ_m(m) is strictly increasing because σ_{m+1}(m+1) ≥ m+1.
For m ≥ p, φ(m) = ψ_p(τ(m)) with τ strictly increasing, so b_p ∘ φ converges.
Every i equals some e(p), so a_{φ(k)}(i) converges.

subproblem.title: Representation of positive linear functionals on C_c(X, ℝ) from Theorem 4.12
subproblem.statement: Assume RieszPositive (Simon Thm 4.12) for spaces in universe u: for every locally compact Hausdorff space Y in universe u and every ℝ≥0-linear λ : C_c(Y, ℝ≥0) → ℝ≥0, there is a Radon outer measure ν on Y with λ(h) = ∫_Y h dν̄ (ν̄ = caratheodoryMeasure ν) for all h ∈ C_c(Y, ℝ≥0). Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff space in universe u, and let Λ : C_c(X, ℝ) → ℝ be ℝ-linear with Λ(f) ≥ 0 whenever f ≥ 0 pointwise. Then there is a Radon outer measure μ on X with Λ(f) = ∫_X f d(caratheodoryMeasure μ) for every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ).
subproblem.lean_statement: RieszPositive.{u} → ∀ (X : Type u) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [LocallyCompactSpace X] (Λ : C_c(X, ℝ) →ₗ[ℝ] ℝ), (∀ f : C_c(X, ℝ), 0 ≤ f → 0 ≤ Λ f) → ∃ μ : OuterMeasure X, IsRadonOuterMeasure μ ∧ ∀ f : C_c(X, ℝ), Λ f = ∫ x, f x ∂caratheodoryMeasure μ
subproblem.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `rc_riesz_real`.
Source: the parent proof of Simon Thm 4.16 (corrected), Step 6: “The restriction of F to K₊ = C_c(X, [0, ∞)) is additive, positively homogeneous and [0, ∞)-valued, i.e. an ℝ≥0-linear map C_c(X, ℝ≥0) → ℝ≥0. By Theorem 4.12 … there is a Radon outer measure μ on X with F(f) = ∫_X f dμ for all f ∈ K₊. For f ∈ C_c(X) write f = f⁺ − f⁻ …”. Here F is replaced by an arbitrary positive linear Λ, and Theorem 4.12 is taken as the hypothesis RieszPositive.

Sibling result used: `rc_cc_integrable` (every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) is μ̄-integrable for a Radon outer measure μ, where μ̄ := caratheodoryMeasure μ).

1. The functional on K₊. For h ∈ C_c(X, ℝ≥0), let h̃ ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) be h regarded as a real-valued function, h̃(x) := h(x) ∈ [0, ∞); it is continuous with the same support. Since h̃ ≥ 0 pointwise, Λ(h̃) ≥ 0, so λ(h) := Λ(h̃) defines a map λ : C_c(X, ℝ≥0) → ℝ≥0.
2. λ is ℝ≥0-linear. For h_1, h_2 ∈ C_c(X, ℝ≥0) and c ∈ ℝ≥0, pointwise (h_1 + h_2)~ = h̃_1 + h̃_2 and (c·h_1)~ = c·h̃_1. By ℝ-linearity of Λ, λ(h_1 + h_2) = λ(h_1) + λ(h_2) and λ(c·h_1) = c·λ(h_1). Thus λ is additive and positively homogeneous, i.e. an ℝ≥0-linear map C_c(X, ℝ≥0) → ℝ≥0.
3. Theorem 4.12. Apply the hypothesis RieszPositive to the locally compact Hausdorff space X and λ. This gives a Radon outer measure μ on X with λ(h) = ∫_X h(x) dμ̄(x) (as real numbers) for every h ∈ C_c(X, ℝ≥0).
4. Positive and negative parts. Let f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ), and put f⁺ := max{f, 0} and f⁻ := max{−f, 0}.
   - They are continuous and [0, ∞)-valued, and {f^± ≠ 0} ⊆ {f ≠ 0}. So their supports are closed subsets of the compact set tsupport f, hence compact: f^± ∈ C_c(X, ℝ≥0).
   - Pointwise f = f⁺ − f⁻, i.e. f = (f⁺)~ − (f⁻)~ in C_c(X, ℝ).
5. Integrability. (f⁺)~ and (f⁻)~ belong to C_c(X, ℝ), so they are μ̄-integrable by `rc_cc_integrable`.
6. Conclusion. By linearity of Λ, Step 3 and Step 5,
   Λ(f) = Λ((f⁺)~) − Λ((f⁻)~) = λ(f⁺) − λ(f⁻) = ∫_X f⁺ dμ̄ − ∫_X f⁻ dμ̄ = ∫_X (f⁺ − f⁻) dμ̄ = ∫_X f dμ̄.
   The fourth equality is additivity of the integral for the integrable functions of Step 5. As f was arbitrary, μ is a Radon outer measure with Λ(f) = ∫_X f dμ̄ for all f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ). ∎

subproblem.title: One subsequence along which all test-function integrals converge
subproblem.statement: Let X be a locally compact Hausdorff, second countable topological space (universe u). Let (μ_k)_{k∈ℕ} be Radon outer measures on X (Simon Def. 4.6) with sup_k μ_k(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ X, and write μ̄_k := caratheodoryMeasure μ_k. Then there is a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ such that for every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) the real sequence (∫_X f dμ̄_{φ(k)})_{k∈ℕ} converges to some l ∈ ℝ.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (X : Type u) [TopologicalSpace X] [T2Space X] [LocallyCompactSpace X] [SecondCountableTopology X] (μ : ℕ → OuterMeasure X), (∀ k, IsRadonOuterMeasure (μ k)) → (∀ K : Set X, IsCompact K → ⨆ k, μ k K < ∞) → ∃ φ : ℕ → ℕ, StrictMono φ ∧ ∀ f : C_c(X, ℝ), ∃ l : ℝ, Tendsto (fun k => ∫ x, f x ∂caratheodoryMeasure (μ (φ k))) atTop (𝓝 l)
subproblem.natural_proof:
PROOF OF `rc_subseq_integrals_converge`.
Source: the parent proof of Simon Thm 4.16 (corrected), Steps 1–4 and the convergence assertion of Step 5: “For f ∈ C_c(X) choose j with spt f ⊆ K_j … ∫_X f dμ_{φ(k)} = F_{j,φ(k)}(f|_{K_j}) converges as k → ∞”.
The parent runs the density argument of Step 4 on all of C(K_j). Step 5 only uses it at restrictions of test functions f with spt f ⊆ K_j, for which F_{j,k}(f|_{K_j}) = ∫_X f dμ̄_k (Step 3). We therefore run Steps 1–4 directly on such test functions, choosing the countable dense set inside that class.

Sibling results used:
- `rc_cc_integrable`: every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) is μ̄-integrable for a Radon outer measure μ.
- `rc_cc_integral_abs_le`: |∫ f dμ̄| ≤ μ(tsupport f)·C whenever |f| ≤ C everywhere.
- `rc_diagonal_subseq`: a diagonal subsequence for countably many bounded real sequences.
- `rc_cc_countable_dense`: a countable uniformly dense family of test functions supported in a compact set, for X Hausdorff and second countable.

1. (Step 1: exhaustion.)
   - X is σ-compact. Every x ∈ X has an open neighbourhood U_x with compact closure (local compactness). A basic open set B with x ∈ B ⊆ U_x has compact closure, being a closed subset of the compact set cl U_x. The countably many basic open sets with compact closure therefore cover X, so X = ⋃_{m≥1} C_m with C_m compact.
   - Put K_1 := C_1. Given a compact K_j, cover the compact set K_j ∪ C_{j+1} by finitely many open sets with compact closures, and let K_{j+1} be the union of their closures.
   - Then each K_j is compact, K_j ∪ C_{j+1} ⊆ int K_{j+1}, and ⋃_j K_j = X.
   - Every compact C ⊆ X lies in some K_j: the open sets int K_{j+1} increase with j and cover X (they contain K_1 = C_1 and every C_{j+1}), so finitely many of them, hence the largest one, cover C.
   - Being compact in a Hausdorff space, each K_j is closed.
2. (Step 2: bounds.) M_j := sup_k μ_k(K_j) < ∞ by hypothesis. For every k and every A ⊆ K_j, monotonicity of the outer measure μ_k gives μ_k(A) ≤ μ_k(K_j) ≤ M_j. All these numbers are finite and are compared as real numbers below.
3. (Step 1: countable dense sets.) X is Hausdorff and second countable, and each K_j is compact. So `rc_cc_countable_dense` gives countable sets D_j ⊆ C_c(X, ℝ) such that:
   - tsupport g ⊆ K_j for every g ∈ D_j;
   - for every ε > 0, every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) with tsupport f ⊆ K_j is within ε at every point of some g ∈ D_j.
   Let D := ⋃_j D_j; D is countable.
4. (Steps 2–3: bounded sequences.) Let g ∈ D, say g ∈ D_j. |g| is bounded on the compact set tsupport g and vanishes outside it, so there is C_g ∈ ℝ with |g(x)| ≤ C_g for all x. By `rc_cc_integral_abs_le` and Step 2 (with A = tsupport g ⊆ K_j), for every k:
   |∫_X g dμ̄_k| ≤ μ_k(tsupport g)·C_g ≤ μ_k(tsupport g)·|C_g| ≤ M_j·|C_g|.
   So for each g ∈ D the real sequence (∫_X g dμ̄_k)_{k∈ℕ} is bounded.
5. (Step 4: diagonal sequence.) Apply `rc_diagonal_subseq` to the countable index set ι := D and a_k(g) := ∫_X g dμ̄_k. This gives a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ such that (∫_X g dμ̄_{φ(k)})_k converges for every g ∈ D.
6. (Step 4 density argument and Step 5.) Let f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ). Its support tsupport f is compact, so by Step 1 there is j with tsupport f ⊆ K_j. We show that (∫_X f dμ̄_{φ(k)})_k is a Cauchy sequence.
   - Let ε > 0 and η := ε/(3(M_j + 1)) > 0, so that M_j·η < ε/3. By Step 3 choose g ∈ D_j with |f(x) − g(x)| ≤ η for all x ∈ X.
   - The function f − g ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) satisfies {f − g ≠ 0} ⊆ {f ≠ 0} ∪ {g ≠ 0} ⊆ tsupport f ∪ tsupport g ⊆ K_j. Since K_j is closed, tsupport(f − g) ⊆ K_j.
   - For every k, f and g are μ̄_k-integrable (`rc_cc_integrable`), so ∫ f dμ̄_k − ∫ g dμ̄_k = ∫ (f − g) dμ̄_k. By `rc_cc_integral_abs_le` (with C = η) and Step 2,
     |∫ f dμ̄_k − ∫ g dμ̄_k| ≤ μ_k(tsupport(f − g))·η ≤ M_j·η < ε/3.
   - Since g ∈ D, the sequence (∫ g dμ̄_{φ(k)})_k converges by Step 5, hence is Cauchy: there is N with |∫ g dμ̄_{φ(m)} − ∫ g dμ̄_{φ(n)}| < ε/3 for all m, n ≥ N.
   - For m, n ≥ N the triangle inequality gives
     |∫ f dμ̄_{φ(m)} − ∫ f dμ̄_{φ(n)}| ≤ |∫ f dμ̄_{φ(m)} − ∫ g dμ̄_{φ(m)}| + |∫ g dμ̄_{φ(m)} − ∫ g dμ̄_{φ(n)}| + |∫ g dμ̄_{φ(n)} − ∫ f dμ̄_{φ(n)}| < ε/3 + ε/3 + ε/3 = ε.
     This is the parent's estimate |F_{j,φ(k)}(g) − F_{j,φ(l)}(g)| ≤ 2M_jη + |F_{j,φ(k)}(g′) − F_{j,φ(l)}(g′)|.
   - Thus the sequence is Cauchy, and as ℝ is complete it converges to some l ∈ ℝ.
7. Conclusion. φ is strictly increasing (Step 5), and for every f ∈ C_c(X, ℝ) the sequence (∫_X f dμ̄_{φ(k)})_k converges (Step 6). ∎
